title: Money, business & hustle
entries: Compound interest
Growth on top of growth. Money earning about 7% a year roughly doubles every 10 years. Time in the market matters more than timing it. Debt compounds the same way, against you.
Rule of 72
Divide 72 by the annual growth rate to estimate the years to double. At 6% it's about 12 years; at 24% credit-card interest your debt doubles in about 3.
Emergency fund
Keep 3 to 6 months of essential expenses in cash before investing aggressively. It turns emergencies into inconveniences and stops you selling investments at the worst time.
Good debt vs bad debt
Debt that buys an asset or skill that pays back more than it costs can be reasonable. High-interest debt for things that lose value (credit cards, car loans on flashy cars) is a wealth killer.
Index funds
Low-cost funds that hold a whole market. Most professional stock pickers fail to beat them over long periods after fees. Boring, diversified, and very hard to beat.
Lifestyle creep
Spending rises to match income, so raises disappear. Fix: when income goes up, automatically save at least half of the increase before you get used to it.
Scams and get-rich-quick
Red flags: guaranteed high returns, pressure to act now, recruiting others, secrecy, payment in gift cards or crypto, and gurus selling courses about how they got rich selling courses.
Revenue vs profit
Revenue is money in; profit is what's left after all costs. Plenty of businesses with big revenue lose money. Cash flow (when money actually arrives) kills more businesses than lack of profit.
Unit economics
What you earn and spend per customer or per sale. If each sale loses money, more sales just lose more money. Know your customer acquisition cost and lifetime value.
Product-market fit
When people want your thing so much they pull it out of your hands: they buy, return, and tell friends without being pushed. Before that, everything else is premature.
Validate before building
Talk to potential customers about their problems (not your idea), get pre-orders or deposits, and sell a simple version before building the full thing. A paying customer beats a hundred compliments.
Pricing
Price on value to the customer, not just your costs. Most beginners undercharge. Raising prices often loses a few customers but increases profit and attracts better ones.
Side hustle first
Build a business on nights and weekends until it reliably covers a meaningful part of your income, then decide about quitting. Quitting first adds desperation, which leads to bad decisions.
Negotiating salary

Research the market rate, let them give a number first if you can, anchor high with evidence, negotiate the whole package (title, remote, bonus, time off), and get it in writing. Most offers have room.
Leverage
Getting more output per unit of effort: code, media, capital, and people. Code and content work while you sleep; hourly work doesn't scale.
Skill stacking
Being in the top 25% at two or three complementary skills (say, sales plus coding plus writing) is often more valuable than being world-class at one.
Marketing basics
Know exactly who it's for, what painful problem it solves, and why you instead of the alternatives. Specific beats general: 'for busy nurses' sells better than 'for everyone'.
Taxes reality

Self-employed income usually means setting aside a chunk of every payment for taxes, often 25 to 30 percent. Track expenses; many business costs are deductible. Rules vary by country, so check locally.
Wealth vs looking rich
Many people who look rich are leveraged and broke; many who are rich look ordinary. Net worth is what you own minus what you owe, not what you drive.
Opportunity in boring businesses
Unsexy industries like cleaning, plumbing, logistics, bookkeeping and repairs often have steady demand, less competition, and solid margins.
